# AIS binding {#sec-binding-ais}

[Normative]{.status}

## Overview

AIS [@itu-m1371] reaches vessels over VHF without any internet connection, ship to ship and ship to shore.
It is valuable precisely where IP is unavailable, but its messages are small and its channel capacity is shared and limited.

This binding covers AIS messages on every transport that carries them:

VHF
: The AIS data link, ship to ship and ship to shore.

Sentences
: On board, AIS messages encapsulated in sentences over NMEA 0183 or IEC 61162-450.

PGNs
: On board, AIS messages carried in PGNs over NMEA 2000 or OneNet.

### Participants

National shore stations
: Shore stations operated by the national authority responsible for aids to navigation.

Private AtoN shore stations
: Shore stations operated by other bodies under private AtoN identifiers, singly or in networks (@sec-ais-trust).

Commercial vessels
: Usually carry Class A stations, which accept messages to transmit from the vessel's network (@sec-ais-constraints).
  Many are required to carry AIS (@tbl-ais-carriage).

Recreational vessels
: Carry Class B stations, AIS receivers or no AIS equipment.
  Class B stations transmit a restricted set of messages, and none is known to accept messages to transmit from the vessel's network (@sec-ais-constraints).
  Some are required to carry AIS (@tbl-ais-carriage).

| Rules | Vessels required to carry AIS | Class |
|:---|:---|:---|
| SOLAS [@imo-ais] | Ships of 300 gross tonnage and upwards on international voyages; cargo ships of 500 gross tonnage and upwards not on international voyages; all passenger ships | Not specified; a Class A station meets the IMO carriage requirement [@itu-m1371] |
| The Bahamas [@bs-act-2025-61] | Foreign-owned vessels of 50 ft and over in Bahamian waters, with AIS on at all times | Not specified |
| Canada [@ca-sor-2020-216] | Vessels of 20 m or more other than pleasure craft; vessels carrying more than 50 passengers, dangerous goods or pollutants in bulk; some dredges; towboats of 8 m or more | Class A |
| | Other passenger-carrying vessels on voyages beyond sheltered waters | Class A or B |
| European Union [@eu-dir-2002-59; @eu-reg-1224-2009] | Passenger ships of any size, and other ships of 300 gross tonnage and upwards, calling at a port of a Member State or on domestic voyages | Not specified; equipment meets the SOLAS requirements |
| | Fishing vessels over 15 m flying a Member State flag, operating in Member State waters or landing catch in a Member State port | Class A |
| United Kingdom [@uk-si-2020-673; @uk-si-2004-2110] | SOLAS requirements, applied to UK ships and to foreign ships in UK waters; fishing vessels over 15 m; some ships on domestic voyages | Not specified; equipment meets the SOLAS requirements |
| United States [@cfr-33-164-46] | Self-propelled commercial vessels of 65 ft or more; towing vessels of 26 ft or more over 600 hp; vessels certificated for more than 150 passengers; some dredging vessels; vessels carrying certain dangerous cargoes | Class A |
| | Some fishing, small passenger and dredging vessels | Class A or B |

: Examples of rules requiring vessels to carry AIS {#tbl-ais-carriage}

A shore station receives the position reports and static data of vessels in range, and can send them addressed and broadcast messages.

### Applications

Applications of this binding include:

- **Management area alerts.** A shore station alerts a vessel that approaches an official management area and meets the area's criteria, such as size and speed, with an addressed message identifying the area and the regulation that applies (@sec-ais-example-area-alert).
- **Sightings.** A shore station relays a sighting to vessels nearby (@sec-app-whales).
- **Notices about sightings.** A shore station relays to vessels nearby a notice that an authority issues about a sighted organism, such as a zone around a whale (@sec-app-whales).
- **Local alerts.** A station broadcasts a short alert to stations in range.

## Transport mechanics

### VHF

#### Getting current state

No mechanism is defined.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Should an ASM be defined for requesting information from another station?
:::

#### Receiving changes

A station receives changes as messages that other stations send unsolicited.

#### Addressing and routing

Broadcast and addressed messages.

#### Constraints {#sec-ais-constraints}

Constraints are from ITU-R M.1371-6 [@itu-m1371]; table numbers refer to that Recommendation.

A slot carries 256 bits.
A message occupies up to 3 slots, or up to 5 slots where FATDMA reservations can be used.

| Message | Maximum content | Content that fits in 1 / 2 / 3 / 5 slots |
|:---|:---|:---|
| 6 Addressed binary | 16-bit application identifier and 920 bits of application data | 8 / 36 / 64 / 117 bytes (Table 53) |
| 8 Binary broadcast | 16-bit application identifier and 952 bits of application data | 12 / 40 / 68 / 121 bytes (Table 56) |
| 12 Safety related addressed | 156 six-bit characters | 10 / 48 / 85 / 156 characters (Table 60) |
| 14 Safety related broadcast | 161 six-bit characters | 16 / 53 / 90 / 161 characters (Table 62) |
| 25 Single slot binary | 1 slot only | 80 to 128 bits, depending on addressing and coding (Table 80) |
| 26 Multiple slot binary | 1 004 bits of data in 5 slots | — |

: AIS message sizes {#tbl-ais-message-sizes}

Class B CS stations (Table 42):

- transmit position reports (message 18) and static data (message 24), and respond to interrogations for them;
- may transmit message 14, entered manually, without pre-formatted text or automatic repetition, in 1 slot (16 characters);
- may transmit message 13 to acknowledge message 12, if they process message 12;
- do not transmit messages 6, 8, 12, 25 or 26.

Class B SO stations:

- transmit messages 6 and 8 in at most 3 slots (64 and 68 bytes);
- transmit message 12 in at most 3 slots (85 characters);
- transmit message 14 in at most 3 slots (90 characters);
- respond to interrogations for messages 18 and 24 (Table 63).

Neither class of Class B station interrogates other stations (Table 63).

To have a message transmitted, an on-board gateway passes it to the AIS station over the vessel's network:

- Class A stations accept messages to transmit over NMEA 0183: an ABM sentence carries an addressed message and a BBM sentence a broadcast message.
  This is confirmed in practice.
- Class A stations that output PGNs over NMEA 2000 may not accept messages to transmit over NMEA 2000.
- No Class B station is known to accept ABM or BBM sentences over NMEA 0183.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How can a gateway on a vessel with Class B equipment have framework messages transmitted over AIS, given that Class B SO stations may transmit messages 6, 8, 12 and 14 but no known Class B station accepts them from the vessel's network?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
ITU-R M.1371-6 has no table of the messages a Class B SO station transmits, as Table 42 does for Class B CS; limits are given message by message.
Which messages besides 6, 8, 12 and 14 can Class B SO stations transmit, and in how many slots?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
ITU-R M.1371-6 is inconsistent for Class B CS and message 12.
Table 42 says a Class B CS station does not transmit message 12, but the description of message 12 limits a Class B CS station to 1 slot (10 characters).
Can a Class B CS station transmit message 12?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="To be written"}
Slot usage and channel load; range; the messages permitted to other station types.
:::

### Sentences

The mechanics are those of the sentence binding's transports, NMEA 0183 and IEC 61162-450 (@sec-binding-sentences).

### PGNs

PGNs carry AIS messages intact, with a PGN for each AIS message type.
The mechanics are those of the PGN binding's transports, NMEA 2000 and OneNet (@sec-binding-pgns).

## Representation

Framework information is carried in AIS messages [@itu-m1371], including:

- **application-specific messages** (ASMs) in the addressed binary message (message 6) and the binary broadcast message (message 8),
  following IMO guidance on their use [@imo-sn1-circ289];
- the **safety related addressed message** (message 12) and the **safety related broadcast message** (message 14).

| Concept | AIS message |
|:---|:---|
| Official management area, announced by a notice | Area Notice or Geographic Notice ASM carrying the notice, with the area's shape; the reference to the management area is not carried |
| Management area alert | Message 12 with text identifying the area and the regulation; an addressed Area Notice ASM (candidate, to be tested) |
| Sighting, from shore to ship | Area Notice ASM whose sub-area is a point |
| Notice about an organism, such as a zone around a sighted whale, from shore to ship | Area Notice or Geographic Notice ASM; the reference to the organism is not carried |
| Local alert | Message 14 with defined text |
| Additional information about any of these | Linked Text ASM (candidate) |
| The IRI of a sighting or notice | Linked Text ASM with the same linkage (proposed, to be tested; @sec-ais-identity) |

: Concepts carried over AIS {#tbl-ais-concepts}

See [provisional decision 0012](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0012-ais-messages-for-concepts.md).

An ASM's name belongs to the transport, not to the concept it carries.
An Area Notice ASM can carry a sighting or a notice, and a sighting it carries is still a sighting, not a notice (@sec-sightings-organisms).
Neither is carried over AIS as a Thing.
What AIS carries are the changes to it (@sec-changes): its creation and its updates, among them a withdrawal, and the expiry scheduled by its duration (@sec-vocab-notices).
A notice of a management area that moves with an organism is carried with the area the zone covers at the time, and each move is an update (@sec-management-areas).
See [provisional decision 0017](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0017-sightings-organisms-notices.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Can an Area Notice also carry a sighting from ship to ship or from ship to shore?
How does a receiver tell whether an Area Notice carries a sighting or a notice: by its point sub-area alone, or also by its description, given that a notice may also be a point?
What do an Area Notice's start time and duration mean when it carries a sighting?
What text does message 14 carry for a local alert?
Which other concepts need AIS messages, and are new ASMs needed for them?
Should a sighting have an ASM of its own, and a defined text when it is sent in an Area Notice? See [proposed decision 0018](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0018-sighting-asm.md).
How are IRIs reduced to identifiers small enough for AIS?
:::

### Identity of sightings and notices {#sec-ais-identity}

Over AIS, a sighting or a notice is identified by an **alias**: the station that transmits it and its linkage identifier, not its IRI.
An alias lasts only as long as its linkage identifier, which a station can reuse for later messages.
One Thing can have several aliases, for example when a network of shore stations transmits one notice from each station.
It loses its references, such as the organism it concerns: an ASM can say that an area concerns marine mammals, but not which one.
A sighting also loses what Darwin Core records of it, such as what was seen, how many and by whom.

To make its identity recoverable ([NCF-SEM-013](../overview/semantic-model.qmd#ncf-sem-013)), a sighting or a notice carried over AIS can also carry its IRI,
for example in a Linked Text ASM with the same linkage.
A receiver with an IP connection can then retrieve the full Thing, with what AIS does not carry.
So that a receiver can match the two, the Thing published over IP states every station and linkage identifier it is carried under ([NCF-BND-AIS-001](#ncf-bnd-ais-001)).

A receiver that hears a sighting or a notice over AIS alone, before it knows its IRI, holds it under a local identifier of its own, marked as incomplete ([NCF-SEM-012](../overview/semantic-model.qmd#ncf-sem-012)).
When it learns the IRI, from a Linked Text or from the Thing published over IP, it identifies the Thing by that IRI from then on,
and treats every alias linked to that IRI as the same Thing ([NCF-BND-AIS-002](#ncf-bnd-ais-002); for notices, [NCF-VOC-NOT-002](../vocab/notices.qmd#ncf-voc-not-002)).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
AIS text is written in six-bit characters, which have no lower-case letters [@itu-m1371].
How is an IRI written in them: are the IRIs carried over AIS limited to those that lower-casing restores, or are they written some other way?
How does a receiver tell a Linked Text that carries an IRI from one that carries words?
Can an Area Notice have more than one Linked Text, one for its words and one for its IRI?
How long can the IRI be, given the slots a Linked Text can occupy (@tbl-ais-message-sizes)?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
What form does a receiver's local identifier take?
This depends on how namespaces are decided ([decision 0006](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0006-namespaces.md)).
How is a Thing marked as incomplete?
:::

## Trust {#sec-ais-trust}

Over VHF, trust comes from regulation: transmissions are monitored and regulated under official policies.
For example, a shore station transmits under a private AtoN identifier.
See [provisional decision 0013](https://github.com/NMEA-Cloud/Framework/blob/main/decisions/0013-trust-over-vhf.md).

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
How are private AtoN identifiers assigned to networks of shore stations, especially networks whose coverage overlaps geographically?
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Persistent signatures will not fit in an ASM. See the open question in @sec-trust-security.
:::

An IRI received over VHF (@sec-ais-identity) is only a claim.
A receiver that retrieves the Thing it names relies on the trust of the JSON-LD binding (@sec-binding-json-ld),
and checks that the Thing states the station and linkage identifier it was heard under ([NCF-BND-AIS-001](#ncf-bnd-ais-001)).

## Requirements

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-ais-001}
**NCF-BND-AIS-001** · *Draft*\
A sighting or notice published over IP that is also carried over AIS SHOULD state every AIS station and linkage identifier it is carried under.
:::

::: {.requirement #ncf-bnd-ais-002}
**NCF-BND-AIS-002** · *Draft*\
A receiver that learns the IRI of a sighting or notice it holds under an AIS alias MUST identify it by that IRI from then on, and MUST treat every alias linked to that IRI as the same Thing.
:::

## Examples

### Management area alert {#sec-ais-example-area-alert}

An official management area has rules for vessels above a given length and speed.
A network of private AtoN shore stations covers the area.

1. A commercial vessel with a Class A station approaches the area.
2. The network receives the vessel's position reports and static data, and finds that the vessel meets the area's criteria.
3. The network sends the vessel a message 12 whose text identifies the area and the regulation that applies.
4. The vessel's Class A station passes the message to the vessel's network, where a display presents it.

::: {.callout-warning title="Open question"}
Should the alert be carried in an Area Notice ASM in message 6 instead of, or as well as, message 12?
The Area Notice ASM is to be tested for this purpose.
How does the alert identify the regulation that applies?
:::
